[Textbook misprint: the stem reads "Kepler's law equal of area" for "Kepler's law of equal areas".]

Kepler's second law, the law of areas: the line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time. Equivalently, the areal velocity of a planet is constant.
A consequence worth stating is that the planet does not move at a uniform speed: when it is nearer the Sun the radius line is short, so the planet must move faster to sweep the same area in the same time, and when it is farther away it moves more slowly.

Kepler's third law, the law of periods: the square of the time period of revolution of a planet around the Sun is proportional to the cube of the semimajor axis of the ellipse traced by the planet.
If \(T\) is the period and \(r\) the length of the semimajor axis,
\(T^{2} \propto r^{3}\)
or \(\dfrac{T^{2}}{r^{3}} = \text{constant}\)
The same constant applies to every planet orbiting the same Sun, which is what makes the law useful for comparing two orbits.

From Newton's law of gravitation \(F = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\), so \(G = \dfrac{Fr^{2}}{m_{1}m_{2}}\).
Substituting dimensions,
\([G] = \dfrac{[\text{M}^{1}\text{L}^{1}\text{T}^{-2}][\text{L}^{2}]}{[\text{M}^{2}]}\)
\(\therefore [G] = [\text{L}^{3}\text{M}^{-1}\text{T}^{-2}]\)

The binding energy of a satellite is the minimum energy that must be supplied to it to free it from the gravitational influence of the planet, that is to take it to infinity where its total energy becomes zero.
A satellite in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) has total energy \(-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\), which is negative and is what binds it. So
Binding energy \(= +\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\)
The negative sign of the total energy is exactly what tells us the satellite is bound; supplying the binding energy raises the total energy to zero.

A geostationary satellite is one that appears fixed in the sky as seen from a point on the Earth's surface. For that to happen it must satisfy three conditions at once:
1. It revolves in the equatorial plane of the Earth.
2. It has the same sense of rotation as the Earth, that is west to east.
3. Its period of revolution equals the Earth's period of rotation about its own axis, one day or 24 hours.
Because it keeps pace exactly with the point below it, it seems stationary, and it is therefore also called a geosynchronous satellite. Such satellites are used for communication, television transmission, telephones and radiowave signal transmission — for example the INSAT group launched by India.

Newton's universal law of gravitation: every particle of matter attracts every other particle of matter with a force which is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
For two bodies of masses \(m_{1}\) and \(m_{2}\) separated by a distance \(r\),
\(F \propto \dfrac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\)
\(\therefore F = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\)
where \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\) is the universal gravitational constant. The force is attractive and acts along the line joining the two bodies.

Escape velocity is the minimum velocity with which a body must be thrown vertically upwards from the surface of the Earth so that it escapes the Earth's gravitational field and never falls back.
Since the gravitational force of the Earth becomes zero only at infinite distance, the body has to reach infinity in order to escape. Equating the total energy at the surface to zero,
\(\dfrac{1}{2}m\mathrm{v}_{e}^{2} - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\)
For the Earth this works out to about 11.2 km/s.

The acceleration due to gravity DECREASES as the altitude increases. At a height \(h\) above the surface the distance from the Earth's centre becomes \(R + h\), so
\(g_{h} = \dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^{2}}\)
and dividing by \(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\) at the surface,
\(g_{h} = \dfrac{gR^{2}}{(R+h)^{2}} = g\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^{-2}\)
For a small altitude, where \(\dfrac{h}{R} \ll 1\), the binomial expansion with higher powers neglected gives the convenient linear form
\(g_{h} \simeq g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)\)
so near the surface \(g\) falls off roughly twice as fast as the fractional gain in height.

The escape speed from the surface of a planet is
\(\mathrm{v}_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR}\)
so it depends only on
1. the MASS \(M\) of the planet, and
2. the RADIUS \(R\) of the planet (equivalently on \(g\) at its surface, since \(g = GM/R^{2}\)).
The most important point is what it does NOT depend on: the mass \(m\) of the escaping body cancels out of the energy equation, so a pebble and a spacecraft need the same escape speed. It is likewise independent of the direction of projection and of the body's shape or composition.

The MASS of a body does not change at all. Mass is the quantity of matter in the body, an intrinsic property, and it is the same on every planet.
The WEIGHT does change. Weight is the gravitational force on the body, \(W = mg\), and \(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\) depends on the mass and radius of the planet the body is standing on. So as we go from one planet to another the weight changes in the ratio of the two planets' values of \(g\):
\(\dfrac{W_{2}}{W_{1}} = \dfrac{g_{2}}{g_{1}} = \dfrac{M_{2}}{M_{1}} \times \left(\dfrac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}\right)^{2}\)

The periodic time of a geostationary satellite is 24 hours, that is one day (\(\approx 8.64 \times 10^{4}\) s).
This is forced by the definition: the satellite can appear stationary above a point on the Earth's surface only if it completes one revolution in exactly the time the Earth takes to complete one rotation about its own axis.

Statement: every particle of matter attracts every other particle of matter with a force which is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, so that \(F = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\).
Vector form: let \(\vec{r}_{1}\) and \(\vec{r}_{2}\) be the position vectors of \(m_{1}\) and \(m_{2}\) from an origin O, so that \(\vec{r}_{21} = \vec{r}_{2} - \vec{r}_{1}\) is the position of \(m_{2}\) relative to \(m_{1}\), with \(\hat{r}_{21}\) the corresponding unit vector and \(r = |\vec{r}_{21}|\). Then the force on \(m_{2}\) due to \(m_{1}\) is
\(\vec{F}_{21} = G\dfrac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}(-\hat{r}_{21})\)
and likewise the force on \(m_{1}\) due to \(m_{2}\) is
\(\vec{F}_{12} = G\dfrac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}(-\hat{r}_{12})\)
The minus sign carries the physics: it makes the force ATTRACTIVE, directed opposite to the outward unit vector. The two forces satisfy \(\vec{F}_{12} = -\vec{F}_{21}\), so they form an action-reaction pair.

The universal gravitational constant \(G\) is the constant of proportionality in Newton's law of gravitation, \(F = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\).
Putting \(m_{1} = m_{2} = 1\) kg and \(r = 1\) m gives \(F = G\), so \(G\) is numerically equal to the force of attraction between two unit masses placed unit distance apart. It is called universal because the same value applies everywhere in the universe, for every pair of bodies.
SI unit: N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\), and its measured value is \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\).

Putting a satellite into orbit needs TWO different things done to it, and a single stage rocket cannot do both.
1. The satellite must first be lifted vertically to the desired height above the Earth's surface. The first stage of the rocket, ignited at the surface, does this.
2. At that height the satellite must then be given a sufficiently large HORIZONTAL (tangential) velocity, so that it goes into orbit instead of falling back. The second stage supplies this tangential thrust once the required height is reached.
A single stage rocket can only give the satellite a velocity along one direction; it cannot both raise the satellite and then turn it and accelerate it horizontally. Staging also lets the spent first stage, with its empty fuel tanks, be discarded, so the remaining fuel is not wasted lifting dead mass. A minimum of two stages is therefore necessary.

Let a satellite be projected horizontally at a height \(h\) with tangential speed \(\mathrm{v}_{h}\), and let \(\mathrm{v}_{c} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R+h}}\) be the critical speed at that height and \(\mathrm{v}_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R+h}}\) the escape speed there. The orbit depends on \(\mathrm{v}_{h}\) as follows.
1. \(\mathrm{v}_{h} = 0\) or very small: the satellite simply falls back to the Earth along a nearly vertical path.
2. \(\mathrm{v}_{h} < \mathrm{v}_{c}\): the path is an ellipse with the centre of the Earth at the FARTHER focus, and the satellite falls back to the Earth because the ellipse intersects the surface.
3. \(\mathrm{v}_{h} = \mathrm{v}_{c}\): the orbit is a CIRCLE concentric with the Earth; this is the condition for a stable circular orbit.
4. \(\mathrm{v}_{c} < \mathrm{v}_{h} < \mathrm{v}_{e}\): the orbit is an ellipse with the centre of the Earth at the NEARER focus, and the satellite stays bound.
5. \(\mathrm{v}_{h} = \mathrm{v}_{e}\): the path is a PARABOLA and the satellite just escapes the Earth's gravitational field.
6. \(\mathrm{v}_{h} > \mathrm{v}_{e}\): the path is a HYPERBOLA and the satellite escapes with speed left over.

Critical velocity is the exact horizontal velocity at which a satellite must be projected at a given height so that it revolves in a stable circular orbit round the Earth.
Consider a satellite of mass \(m\) revolving in a circular orbit of radius \(r = R + h\) round the Earth of mass \(M\), with speed \(\mathrm{v}_{c}\).
The necessary centripetal force is supplied entirely by the gravitational attraction of the Earth, so
Centripetal force = Gravitational force
\(\dfrac{m\mathrm{v}_{c}^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{c}^{2} = \dfrac{GM}{r}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{c} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R+h}}\)
Notice that \(m\) cancels, so the critical velocity does not depend on the mass of the satellite. Using \(GM = gR^{2}\) it may also be written
\(\mathrm{v}_{c} = R\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R+h}}\)
and for a satellite very close to the surface, where \(h \ll R\),
\(\mathrm{v}_{c} = \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.92\) km/s, the maximum possible critical speed.

A communication satellite is a geostationary satellite: it revolves in the equatorial plane with the same sense and the same period of rotation as the Earth, so it appears stationary from the ground. Four applications are:
1. Communication — relaying telephone and radiowave signals between distant points on the Earth.
2. Television transmission — broadcasting television signals over a wide area.
3. Telephone and data links between continents.
4. Radiowave signal transmission for navigation and broadcasting services.
The INSAT group of satellites launched by India is an example of this class.

Let \(M\) and \(R\) be the mass and radius of the Earth. For a body on the surface, the acceleration due to gravity is
\(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\) --- (1)
When the body is at a height \(h\) above the surface, its distance from the centre of the Earth becomes \(R + h\), so the acceleration due to gravity there is
\(g_{h} = \dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^{2}}\) --- (2)
Dividing (2) by (1),
\(\dfrac{g_{h}}{g} = \dfrac{\dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^{2}}}{\dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}} = \dfrac{R^{2}}{(R+h)^{2}}\)
\(\therefore g_{h} = g\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^{2}\)
which is the required result. Since \(R + h > R\), the bracket is less than one, so \(g_{h} < g\): the acceleration due to gravity goes on decreasing as the altitude increases.

The diagram should show the Earth as a sphere with a point of projection P at a height \(h\) above its surface, and several paths leaving P horizontally, each labelled by its tangential projection speed \(\mathrm{v}_{h}\). Taking \(\mathrm{v}_{c}\) as the critical speed at that height and \(\mathrm{v}_{e} = \sqrt{2}\,\mathrm{v}_{c}\) as the escape speed, the trajectories to be drawn and labelled are:
1. \(\mathrm{v}_{h}\) small — a short arc curving straight back into the Earth's surface (the satellite falls back).
2. \(\mathrm{v}_{h} < \mathrm{v}_{c}\) — an ellipse with the centre of the Earth at the FARTHER focus; this ellipse cuts the Earth's surface, so the satellite again falls back.
3. \(\mathrm{v}_{h} = \mathrm{v}_{c}\) — a CIRCLE concentric with the Earth, the stable circular orbit.
4. \(\mathrm{v}_{c} < \mathrm{v}_{h} < \mathrm{v}_{e}\) — an ellipse with the centre of the Earth at the NEARER focus, the point of projection now being the perigee.
5. \(\mathrm{v}_{h} = \mathrm{v}_{e}\) — an open PARABOLA; the satellite just escapes.
6. \(\mathrm{v}_{h} > \mathrm{v}_{e}\) — an open HYPERBOLA, escaping with speed to spare.
All six paths start at the same point P and are drawn tangential to the horizontal there, so that the ordering of the curves shows how the orbit opens out as the projection speed is increased. (This is the content of Fig. 5.10 of the chapter.)

Consider a body of mass \(m\) lying AT REST on the surface of the Earth, of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\).
Since the body is at rest, its kinetic energy is
\(K.E. = 0\)
Its gravitational potential energy, with the zero of potential energy taken at infinity, is
\(P.E. = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}\)
Hence the total energy of the body is
\(T.E. = K.E. + P.E. = 0 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}\)
The total energy is negative, which is precisely the statement that the body is BOUND to the Earth. To free it, its total energy must be raised to zero, so the minimum energy that has to be supplied is
Binding energy \(= +\dfrac{GMm}{R}\)
Using \(GM = gR^{2}\) this may also be written
Binding energy \(= mgR\)
Note that this is TWICE the binding energy \(\dfrac{GMm}{2R}\) of a satellite of the same mass orbiting close to the surface, because the orbiting satellite already possesses kinetic energy that the resting body does not.

We do not feel our weight directly; what we feel is the NORMAL REACTION \(N\) exerted on us by the floor, which is what a weighing machine records.
For an astronaut of mass \(m\) inside a satellite orbiting at radius \(r\), both the astronaut and the satellite move on the same circular path with the same centripetal acceleration, which is supplied entirely by gravity:
\(a = \dfrac{GM}{r^{2}} = g_{h}\)
Writing Newton's second law for the astronaut in the radial direction,
\(mg_{h} - N = ma = mg_{h}\)
\(\therefore N = 0\)
So the floor of the satellite presses on the astronaut with no force at all, and the astronaut presses on the floor with none either. Since the sensation of weight comes from that reaction, the astronaut feels weightless and floats inside the cabin.
It is important to see that this is NOT because gravity has vanished — at a few hundred kilometres up, \(g_{h}\) is still close to its surface value. The astronaut and the satellite are simply in free fall together, falling around the Earth at the same rate, so there is no relative force between them.

The graph plots the acceleration due to gravity on the vertical axis against distance from the centre of the Earth (or, equivalently, depth below and altitude above the surface) on the horizontal axis. It has two distinct branches meeting at the surface.
1. INSIDE the Earth, for depth \(d\) below the surface, \(g_{d} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)\). Written in terms of the distance \(r = R - d\) from the centre this is \(g_{d} = \dfrac{g}{R}r\), a STRAIGHT LINE through the origin. So the curve rises linearly from \(g_{d} = 0\) at the centre to \(g_{d} = g\) at the surface.
2. OUTSIDE the Earth, for altitude \(h\), \(g_{h} = \dfrac{gR^{2}}{(R+h)^{2}}\), which falls off as the INVERSE SQUARE of the distance from the centre. So beyond the surface the curve falls away as a smooth hyperbola-like decay, approaching zero asymptotically as \(h\) becomes very large but never reaching it.
The two branches meet at the surface, where both give the same value \(g\), and that is the MAXIMUM of the whole graph. The key contrast to label is that \(g\) decreases in BOTH directions from the surface, but linearly going inwards and as an inverse square going outwards. (This is Fig. 5.8 of the chapter.)

The acceleration due to gravity is maximum at the POLES.
There are two independent reasons, and both act in the same direction.
1. SHAPE. The Earth is not a perfect sphere but an ellipsoid bulged at the equator, so the polar radius (about 6356 km) is smaller than the equatorial radius (about 6378 km). Since \(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\), the smaller distance from the centre at the pole gives the larger value of \(g\).
2. ROTATION. The Earth's rotation about its axis reduces the effective value of \(g\) by a centrifugal term \(\omega^{2}R\cos^{2}\lambda\), where \(\lambda\) is the latitude. At the poles \(\lambda = 90^\circ\), so \(\cos\lambda = 0\) and this reduction is exactly ZERO — a point on the axis of rotation does not go round in a circle at all.
So the poles both sit closest to the centre and suffer no rotational reduction, and \(g\) is largest there, about 9.83 m/s\(^{2}\).

On the Earth's surface the acceleration due to gravity is minimum at the EQUATOR.
The two reasons are the mirror image of those that make it maximum at the poles.
1. SHAPE. The Earth is bulged at the equator, so the equatorial radius (about 6378 km) is the LARGEST distance from the centre of the Earth to the surface. Since \(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\), the largest radius gives the smallest value of \(g\).
2. ROTATION. The reduction in effective gravity caused by the Earth's rotation is \(\omega^{2}R\cos^{2}\lambda\), which is greatest at latitude \(\lambda = 0^\circ\), that is on the equator, where a point traces the largest circle in a day.
Both effects therefore reduce \(g\) at the equator, giving about 9.78 m/s\(^{2}\) there.
(If points below the surface are also admitted, \(g\) falls to zero at the CENTRE of the Earth, which is its least value anywhere; but on the surface itself the minimum is at the equator.)

Definition: the binding energy of a satellite is the minimum energy that must be supplied to it in order to free it from the gravitational influence of the planet, that is to take it to infinity where its total energy is zero.
Consider a satellite of mass \(m\) revolving at a height \(h\) above the Earth's surface, so that the orbital radius is \(r = R + h\), with critical velocity \(\mathrm{v}_{c}\).
Kinetic energy: the gravitational force provides the centripetal force, so \(\dfrac{m\mathrm{v}_{c}^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}\), giving \(\mathrm{v}_{c}^{2} = \dfrac{GM}{r}\). Hence
\(K.E. = \dfrac{1}{2}m\mathrm{v}_{c}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{GMm}{r}\)
Potential energy: the gravitational potential at distance \(r\) is \(-\dfrac{GM}{r}\), so
\(P.E. = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}\)
Total energy:
\(T.E. = K.E. + P.E. = \dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{GMm}{r} - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{GMm}{r}\)
The total energy is NEGATIVE, which is what shows that the satellite is bound to the Earth. To unbind it the total energy must be raised to zero, so the energy to be supplied is
Binding energy \(= +\dfrac{GMm}{2r} = \dfrac{GMm}{2(R+h)}\)
Using \(GM = gR^{2}\), this may also be written \(\dfrac{mgR^{2}}{2(R+h)}\).

Imagine the Earth as a sphere of radius \(R\) and uniform density \(\rho\), made of a large number of concentric shells.
On the SURFACE, taking the whole mass \(M\) as concentrated at the centre,
\(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\), and with \(M = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\rho\) this becomes
\(g = \dfrac{G \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\rho}{R^{2}} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R\rho G\) --- (1)
Now take a point P at a DEPTH \(d\) below the surface, so that its distance from the centre is \(R - d\). The material lying OUTSIDE the sphere through P — the shell above — exerts no net gravitational force at P, because the force at any point inside a uniform hollow shell is zero. Only the inner sphere of radius \(R - d\) contributes, and its mass is
\(M' = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (R-d)^{3}\rho\)
so
\(g_{d} = \dfrac{GM'}{(R-d)^{2}} = \dfrac{G \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (R-d)^{3}\rho}{(R-d)^{2}} = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (R-d)\rho G\) --- (2)
Dividing (2) by (1),
\(\dfrac{g_{d}}{g} = \dfrac{R-d}{R} = 1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\)
\(\therefore g_{d} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)\)
This is the required formula. It shows that \(g\) decreases LINEARLY with depth, and that at the centre, where \(d = R\), the acceleration due to gravity is zero.

Kepler's three laws of planetary motion are:
1. LAW OF ORBIT. Every planet moves in an elliptical orbit around the Sun, with the Sun situated at one of the two foci of the ellipse.
2. LAW OF AREAS. The line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time, that is the areal velocity of the planet is constant. A consequence is that a planet moves faster when it is nearer the Sun and slower when it is farther away.
3. LAW OF PERIODS. The square of the time period of revolution of a planet around the Sun is proportional to the cube of the semimajor axis of its elliptical orbit:
\(T^{2} \propto r^{3}\), or \(\dfrac{T^{2}}{r^{3}} = \text{constant}\)
Kepler derived all three from careful observation of the planets; he did not explain WHY the planets obey them. That explanation came later from Newton's universal law of gravitation.

The two formulae are:
At DEPTH \(d\) below the surface: \(g_{d} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)\)
At ALTITUDE \(h\) above the surface: \(g_{h} = \dfrac{gR^{2}}{(R+h)^{2}} = g\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^{-2}\), and for \(h \ll R\) this reduces, on expanding binomially and neglecting higher powers of \(\dfrac{h}{R}\), to \(g_{h} \simeq g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)\).
Now take the ratio, using the small-altitude form as the question permits:
\(\dfrac{g_{d}}{g_{h}} = \dfrac{g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)}{g\left(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right)}\)
Writing each bracket over the common denominator \(R\),
\(= \dfrac{\dfrac{R-d}{R}}{\dfrac{R-2h}{R}}\)
The factors of \(R\) cancel, leaving
\(\therefore \dfrac{g_{d}}{g_{h}} = \dfrac{R-d}{R-2h}\)
which is the required result.

CRITICAL VELOCITY is the exact horizontal (tangential) velocity that must be given to a satellite at a given height so that it revolves in a stable CIRCULAR orbit round the Earth. If the speed is less the satellite spirals back to the Earth; if it is more the orbit opens out into an ellipse.
Derivation. Let a satellite of mass \(m\) revolve in a circular orbit of radius \(r = R + h\) with speed \(\mathrm{v}_{c}\) round the Earth of mass \(M\). The gravitational attraction supplies exactly the centripetal force needed:
\(\dfrac{m\mathrm{v}_{c}^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{c}^{2} = \dfrac{GM}{r}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{c} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R+h}}\)
Substituting \(GM = gR^{2}\) gives the equivalent form \(\mathrm{v}_{c} = R\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R+h}}\).
Factors it depends on:
1. the MASS \(M\) of the Earth (or planet);
2. the RADIUS \(R\) of the Earth, and the HEIGHT \(h\) of the orbit — that is, on the orbital radius \(r = R + h\); the critical speed DECREASES as the height increases;
3. equivalently, on the acceleration due to gravity at that altitude.
It does NOT depend on the mass of the satellite, which cancels out of the equation. For an orbit very close to the surface, \(\mathrm{v}_{c} = \sqrt{gR} \approx 7.92\) km/s, and this is the maximum possible critical speed.

DEFINITION. Escape speed is the minimum speed with which a body must be thrown vertically upwards from the surface of the Earth so that it escapes the Earth's gravitational field and does not fall back.
Derivation. Since the gravitational force of the Earth becomes zero only at an infinite distance, the body must be able to reach infinity. Let a body of mass \(m\) be projected with speed \(\mathrm{v}_{e}\) from the surface of the Earth of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\).
On the surface:
\(K.E. = \dfrac{1}{2}m\mathrm{v}_{e}^{2}\)
\(P.E. = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}\)
\(\therefore\) Total energy \(= \dfrac{1}{2}m\mathrm{v}_{e}^{2} - \dfrac{GMm}{R}\)
At infinity, the kinetic energy has just been used up and the potential energy vanishes:
\(K.E. = 0\) and \(P.E. = -\dfrac{GMm}{\infty} = 0\)
\(\therefore\) Total energy at infinity \(= 0\)
Since gravity is a conservative force, energy is conserved between the two states:
\(\dfrac{1}{2}m\mathrm{v}_{e}^{2} - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{1}{2}m\mathrm{v}_{e}^{2} = \dfrac{GMm}{R}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\)
Using \(GM = gR^{2}\) this is also \(\mathrm{v}_{e} = \sqrt{2gR}\). The mass \(m\) of the body cancels, so the escape speed is the same for every body; for the Earth its numerical value is about 11.2 km/s.

Launching a satellite requires two separate things to be done to it — it must be RAISED to the required height, and it must then be given a large HORIZONTAL velocity — and this is why a minimum of two rocket stages is used. A single stage rocket cannot achieve both.
The sequence is as follows.
1. The satellite is mounted on top of the rocket, and the fuel of the FIRST stage is ignited on the surface of the Earth. This stage lifts the rocket vertically upwards and raises the satellite to the desired height above the Earth's surface.
2. When its fuel is exhausted, the first stage — now only empty dead mass — is DETACHED and falls away, so that no further fuel is wasted lifting it.
3. At the required height the rocket is turned so as to move horizontally, and the SECOND stage is ignited. Its thrust supplies the necessary tangential (horizontal) velocity to the satellite.
4. The second stage is fired until the satellite attains the CRITICAL VELOCITY \(\mathrm{v}_{c} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R+h}}\) appropriate to that height. At that instant the satellite is released from the rocket.
5. Thereafter the gravitational attraction of the Earth supplies exactly the centripetal force needed, and the satellite continues to revolve in a stable circular orbit round the Earth without any further propulsion.
If the tangential speed at release is smaller than the critical velocity the satellite falls back to the Earth, and if it is larger the orbit becomes elliptical, so the timing of the release is critical.

Given: \(R = 6400\) km, and \(g\) decreases by 10% so \(g_{d} = 0.9\,g\). To find: the depth \(d\).
At a depth \(d\) below the surface,
\(g_{d} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{g_{d}}{g} = 1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\)
\(\therefore 0.9 = 1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{d}{R} = 0.1\)
\(\therefore d = 0.1 \times 6400\)
\(\therefore d = 640\) km
So the acceleration due to gravity falls by 10% at a depth of 640 km below the Earth's surface.
(Compare Solved Ex.5.7, where the same 10% reduction occurs at a height of only 320 km — half as far — because with altitude \(g\) falls as \(1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\) but with depth only as \(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\).)

Given: the wooden Earth has mass \(M_{w} = 0.1\,M\) with the diameter, and hence the radius \(R\), unchanged. Escape speed from the real Earth \(\mathrm{v}_{e} = 11.2\) km/s. To find: the escape speed \(\mathrm{v}_{w}\) from the wooden Earth.
The escape speed from a body of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) is
\(\mathrm{v}_{e} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}\)
Since \(R\) is the same for both, \(\mathrm{v}_{e} \propto \sqrt{M}\), so
\(\dfrac{\mathrm{v}_{w}}{\mathrm{v}_{e}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_{w}}{M}} = \sqrt{0.1}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{w} = 11.2 \times \sqrt{0.1}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{w} = 11.2 \times 0.3162\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{w} = 3.54\) km/s
So the escape speed from the wooden Earth would be about 3.54 km/s. Note that although the mass falls to one tenth, the escape speed falls only to \(1/\sqrt{10}\) of its value, because of the square root.

[Textbook answer-key error, and the printed key contradicts ITSELF: it gives the potential energy as \(-80.09 \times 10^{9}\) J and the total energy as \(-40.07 \times 10^{9}\) J, while also printing the binding energy as \(40.02 \times 10^{9}\) J. Binding energy is by definition the magnitude of the total energy, so those last two cannot both be right. With \(r = R_{E} + h = 10^{4}\) km, \(\text{PE} = -\dfrac{GM_{E}m}{r} = -80.04 \times 10^{9}\) J and \(\text{TE} = -40.02 \times 10^{9}\) J — which is exactly the binding energy the key itself prints. The kinetic and binding energies are correct; the potential and total energies each carry a digit error.]

Given: \(m = 2000\) kg, \(h = 3600\) km \(= 3.6 \times 10^{6}\) m, \(R = 6400\) km \(= 6.4 \times 10^{6}\) m, \(M = 6 \times 10^{24}\) kg, \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\).
Orbital radius:
\(r = R + h = 6.4 \times 10^{6} + 3.6 \times 10^{6} = 1.0 \times 10^{7}\) m
First evaluate the common factor:
\(GMm = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24} \times 2000 = 8.004 \times 10^{17}\)
KINETIC ENERGY. For a circular orbit the gravitational force supplies the centripetal force, so \(\mathrm{v}_{c}^{2} = \dfrac{GM}{r}\) and
\(K.E. = \dfrac{1}{2}m\mathrm{v}_{c}^{2} = \dfrac{GMm}{2r} = \dfrac{8.004 \times 10^{17}}{2 \times 10^{7}}\)
\(\therefore K.E. = 4.002 \times 10^{10}\) J \(= 40.02 \times 10^{9}\) J
POTENTIAL ENERGY.
\(P.E. = -\dfrac{GMm}{r} = -\dfrac{8.004 \times 10^{17}}{10^{7}}\)
\(\therefore P.E. = -8.004 \times 10^{10}\) J \(= -80.04 \times 10^{9}\) J
TOTAL ENERGY.
\(T.E. = K.E. + P.E. = 40.02 \times 10^{9} - 80.04 \times 10^{9}\)
\(\therefore T.E. = -40.02 \times 10^{9}\) J
BINDING ENERGY. This is the energy needed to raise the total energy to zero, so it is the magnitude of the total energy:
\(B.E. = |T.E.| = 40.02 \times 10^{9}\) J
As a check, note that \(K.E.\) and \(B.E.\) come out equal and \(P.E.\) is exactly twice \(T.E.\) — both are general properties of any circular orbit, since each of these quantities is \(\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\) up to a sign.

Given: \(T_{A} = 1\) hour, \(T_{B} = 8\) hours, \(r_{B} = 4 \times 10^{4}\) km. To find: \(r_{A}\).
Both satellites orbit the SAME planet, so Kepler's law of periods applies to the pair:
\(\dfrac{T_{A}^{2}}{T_{B}^{2}} = \dfrac{r_{A}^{3}}{r_{B}^{3}}\)
\(\therefore \left(\dfrac{r_{A}}{r_{B}}\right)^{3} = \left(\dfrac{T_{A}}{T_{B}}\right)^{2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{64}\)
Taking the cube root of both sides,
\(\dfrac{r_{A}}{r_{B}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{64}\right)^{1/3} = \dfrac{1}{4}\)
\(\therefore r_{A} = \dfrac{4 \times 10^{4}}{4}\)
\(\therefore r_{A} = 1 \times 10^{4}\) km
So satellite A orbits at a radius of \(1 \times 10^{4}\) km. The shorter period goes with the smaller orbit, as it must.

Given: \(M_{S} = 1.99 \times 10^{30}\) kg, \(M_{E} = 5.98 \times 10^{24}\) kg, \(r = 1.5 \times 10^{11}\) m, \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\).
By Newton's law of gravitation,
\(F = \dfrac{GM_{S}M_{E}}{r^{2}}\)
\(\therefore F = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.99 \times 10^{30} \times 5.98 \times 10^{24}}{(1.5 \times 10^{11})^{2}}\)
Numerator \(= 6.67 \times 1.99 \times 5.98 \times 10^{-11+30+24} = 79.38 \times 10^{43} = 7.938 \times 10^{44}\)
Denominator \(= 2.25 \times 10^{22}\)
\(\therefore F = \dfrac{7.938 \times 10^{44}}{2.25 \times 10^{22}}\)
\(\therefore F = 3.53 \times 10^{22}\) N
The gravitational force of attraction between the Sun and the Earth is about \(3.5 \times 10^{22}\) N, and it is this force that keeps the Earth in its orbit.

[Textbook note (not an error): the printed key \(8.889\) m/s\(^{2}\) differs from the exact value \(8.885\) m/s\(^{2}\) by 0.05%, which is intermediate-step rounding rather than a mistake. Recorded so it is not chased later.]

Given: \(h = 300\) km \(= 3 \times 10^{5}\) m, \(M = 5.98 \times 10^{24}\) kg, \(R = 6400\) km \(= 6.4 \times 10^{6}\) m, \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\).
Here \(h\) is not negligible compared with \(R\), so use the exact form rather than the small-altitude approximation:
\(g_{h} = \dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^{2}}\)
Distance from the centre:
\(R + h = 6.4 \times 10^{6} + 0.3 \times 10^{6} = 6.7 \times 10^{6}\) m
\(\therefore g_{h} = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.98 \times 10^{24}}{(6.7 \times 10^{6})^{2}}\)
Numerator \(= 39.89 \times 10^{13} = 3.989 \times 10^{14}\)
Denominator \(= 44.89 \times 10^{12} = 4.489 \times 10^{13}\)
\(\therefore g_{h} = \dfrac{3.989 \times 10^{14}}{4.489 \times 10^{13}}\)
\(\therefore g_{h} = 8.89\) m/s\(^{2}\)
So at 300 km above the surface the acceleration due to gravity is about 8.89 m/s\(^{2}\), appreciably less than its surface value of about 9.8 m/s\(^{2}\).

Given: \(h = 1000\) km \(= 1 \times 10^{6}\) m, \(M_{E} = 5.98 \times 10^{24}\) kg, \(R = 6.4 \times 10^{6}\) m, \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\).
The speed of a satellite in a circular orbit is its critical velocity,
\(\mathrm{v}_{c} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R+h}}\)
Orbital radius:
\(R + h = 6.4 \times 10^{6} + 1 \times 10^{6} = 7.4 \times 10^{6}\) m
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{c} = \sqrt{\dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 5.98 \times 10^{24}}{7.4 \times 10^{6}}}\)
\(= \sqrt{\dfrac{3.989 \times 10^{14}}{7.4 \times 10^{6}}}\)
\(= \sqrt{5.39 \times 10^{7}}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{c} = 7.34 \times 10^{3}\) m/s
So the satellite moves at about 7.34 km/s. This is a little less than the 7.92 km/s that a satellite skimming the surface would need, as expected, since the critical velocity decreases as the height of the orbit increases.

Given: radius of Mars \(R = 3.4 \times 10^{3}\) km \(= 3.4 \times 10^{6}\) m, mass of Mars \(M = 6.4 \times 10^{23}\) kg, \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\).
On the surface of a planet,
\(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\)
\(\therefore g = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.4 \times 10^{23}}{(3.4 \times 10^{6})^{2}}\)
Numerator \(= 42.69 \times 10^{12} = 4.269 \times 10^{13}\)
Denominator \(= 11.56 \times 10^{12} = 1.156 \times 10^{13}\)
\(\therefore g = \dfrac{4.269 \times 10^{13}}{1.156 \times 10^{13}}\)
\(\therefore g = 3.69\) m/s\(^{2}\)
So the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of Mars is about 3.69 m/s\(^{2}\), roughly 38% of its value on the Earth.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key \(5.02 \times 10^{10}\) J is exactly \(\dfrac{GMm}{2R}\), which is the binding energy of a satellite already IN ORBIT close to the surface — a body that has kinetic energy to begin with. This question specifies an object ON the surface, at rest, so the energy needed to remove it to infinity is the full \(\dfrac{GMm}{R} = 1.004 \times 10^{11}\) J, twice the printed value. The distinction is one the book itself sets up: its Q.3 (v) asks the student to derive the binding energy of a body at rest on the surface.]

Given: \(M = 6.4 \times 10^{24}\) kg, \(R = 3.4 \times 10^{6}\) m, \(m = 800\) kg, \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\).
The object is AT REST on the surface, so its kinetic energy is zero and its total energy is entirely potential:
\(K.E. = 0\)
\(P.E. = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}\)
\(\therefore T.E. = -\dfrac{GMm}{R}\)
To remove it to infinity its total energy must be raised to zero, so the energy required is the magnitude of that total energy — the binding energy of a body at rest on the surface:
\(E = \dfrac{GMm}{R}\)
\(\therefore E = \dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.4 \times 10^{24} \times 800}{3.4 \times 10^{6}}\)
Numerator \(= 6.67 \times 6.4 \times 800 \times 10^{13} = 3.415 \times 10^{17}\)
\(\therefore E = \dfrac{3.415 \times 10^{17}}{3.4 \times 10^{6}}\)
\(\therefore E = 1.004 \times 10^{11}\) J
So about \(1.00 \times 10^{11}\) J is required.
[Note: the printed answer to this question, \(5.02 \times 10^{10}\) J, is exactly half of this, and equals \(\dfrac{GMm}{2R}\) — the binding energy of a satellite ORBITING close to the surface, which already possesses kinetic energy. For a body at rest on the surface, which is what this question specifies, the required energy is \(\dfrac{GMm}{R}\), as the book's own Ex Q.3 (v) asks the student to derive.]

Given: \(M = 6 \times 10^{24}\) kg, \(R = 6400\) km \(= 6.4 \times 10^{6}\) m, \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\). To find: \(G\).
On the surface of the Earth,
\(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\)
Rearranging for \(G\),
\(G = \dfrac{gR^{2}}{M}\)
\(\therefore G = \dfrac{9.8 \times (6.4 \times 10^{6})^{2}}{6 \times 10^{24}}\)
\(= \dfrac{9.8 \times 4.096 \times 10^{13}}{6 \times 10^{24}}\)
\(= \dfrac{4.014 \times 10^{14}}{6 \times 10^{24}}\)
\(\therefore G = 6.69 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\)
This agrees well with the accepted value \(6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\); the small difference comes from the rounded values of \(M\) and \(R\) supplied in the question.

Given: weight on the Earth \(W_{E} = 5.6\) kg wt; for the planet \(M_{P} = 7M_{E}\) and \(R_{P} = 2R_{E}\). To find: the weight \(W_{P}\) on the planet.
The MASS of the body is unchanged; only \(g\) differs. On any body of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\),
\(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\)
so
\(\dfrac{g_{P}}{g_{E}} = \dfrac{M_{P}}{M_{E}} \times \left(\dfrac{R_{E}}{R_{P}}\right)^{2} = 7 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{7}{4} = 1.75\)
Since weight \(W = mg\) with the same \(m\),
\(\dfrac{W_{P}}{W_{E}} = \dfrac{g_{P}}{g_{E}} = 1.75\)
\(\therefore W_{P} = 5.6 \times 1.75\)
\(\therefore W_{P} = 9.8\) kg-wt
So the body would weigh 9.8 kg-wt on that planet. Note that the seven-fold gain in mass is partly offset by the doubling of the radius, which divides \(g\) by four.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \(2.08 \times 10^{7}\) J. The magnitude is right but two things are wrong with it. Gravitational potential is always NEGATIVE, approaching zero only at infinity, so the value is \(-2.08 \times 10^{7}\); and its SI unit is J/kg, not J, because potential is the potential energy PER UNIT MASS.]

Given: height above the surface \(= 2R_{E}\), \(M = 6 \times 10^{24}\) kg, \(R_{E} = 6400\) km \(= 6.4 \times 10^{6}\) m, \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\) kg\(^{-2}\).
First find the distance of the point FROM THE CENTRE of the Earth. The height is measured from the SURFACE, so
\(r = R_{E} + 2R_{E} = 3R_{E} = 3 \times 6.4 \times 10^{6} = 1.92 \times 10^{7}\) m
The gravitational potential at a distance \(r\) from the centre of the Earth is
\(V = -\dfrac{GM}{r}\)
\(\therefore V = -\dfrac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6 \times 10^{24}}{1.92 \times 10^{7}}\)
\(= -\dfrac{4.002 \times 10^{14}}{1.92 \times 10^{7}}\)
\(\therefore V = -2.08 \times 10^{7}\) J/kg
Two points are worth stressing. The potential is NEGATIVE, as gravitational potential always is, approaching zero only at infinity. And its SI unit is J/kg, not J, because potential is the potential energy PER UNIT MASS — the potential energy of a body of mass \(m\) placed there would be \(V \times m\) joules.
